9214-GBR: Welcomes adoption of 2664 and preserves UK support, favourable vote and sponsorship.
The United Kingdom is pleased to have voted in favour and to have been a sponsor of resolution 2664 (2022).
Retains sanctions as a legitimate Charter-based Council tool, rather than renouncing sanctions.
In line with the Charter of the United Nations, they are rightly used to address threats to international peace and security.
Carveout is for specified organizations and necessary humanitarian/basic-needs activities under UN asset freezes; not unrestricted transfers to designated entities.

The resolution will provide that certain activities necessary for humanitarian assistance or in support of basic human needs, when carried out by specified organizations, do not violate United Nations asset freezes.
Explains clarity for humanitarian providers and their service providers and effective aid delivery.
The resolution will help save lives by providing clarity, to help ensure that humanitarian providers and their service providers can continue to help the most vulnerable.
9214-IND: Sanctions remain provisional, not ends in themselves; humanitarian and legitimate economic effects matter.
The measures imposed by the Security Council under Article 41 of the Charter of the United Nations are provisional in nature and not permanent.
India engaged constructively on 2664 and acknowledges the humanitarian/basic-needs carveout.
In that context, India engaged constructively in the negotiations on resolution 2664 (2022).
Retains concern about terrorist groups masquerading as humanitarian/civil-society groups to evade sanctions, raise funds and recruit fighters.
Those terrorist organizations use the umbrella of the humanitarian assistance space to raise funds and recruit fighters.
Exemptions must not facilitate political mainstreaming of terror entities; due diligence remains essential.
More important, such exemptions must not facilitate the mainstreaming of terror entities in the political space in our region.
India sought proactive 1267 Monitoring Team/reporting safeguards; concerns were NOT fully addressed and correction is a future hope.
We regret that those specific concerns were not fully addressed in the final text adopted today.
8923-IND: Supports adequate, sustainable resources, training and logistics for G-5 Sahel security efforts.
A resource-constrained counter-terrorism strategy can be a recipe for failure.
Opposes a separate Council climate/security track in favour of inclusive UNFCCC mechanisms, while recognizing climate harms; not climate denial.

Given that background, we do not think that it is appropriate to draw a separate link between security and climate change, especially when all aspects of climate change are already being dealt with holistically
Attributes contested climate-violence causation to India's account, avoiding an invented universal scientific finding that climate has no security effects.
The report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change clearly states that the effect of climate variability on violence is contested.

Preserves the five announced goals and horizons: intensity 45% vs 2005 by 2030; installed non-fossil electricity 50% by 2030; projected emissions down 1bn tons by 2030; non-fossil energy 500GW by 2030; net zero 2070.
achieving the target of net zero by the year 2070
Developed-country finance and technology obligations are not shifted to developing countries; $1tn is urged, not already delivered.
urge developed countries to begin providing climate financing of $1 trillion at the earliest.
Concludes that terrorism and climate each have established institutional mechanisms and should be addressed through them.
today we have institutional mechanisms to address each of these issues.
8923-GBR: Treats climate as a threat multiplier for vulnerable/conflict-affected populations, avoiding deterministic climate-causes-all-terrorism claims.
the impacts of climate change act as a multiplier of the threats already facing vulnerable populations.
Accurately treats COP26 commitments as commitments, including 1.5C hope, adaptation financing and $100bn by 2023 at the latest.
meeting the $100 billion goal by 2023 at the latest.
Calls for UN climate/security reporting and a CTED role.
Secondly, we need the United Nations system to report comprehensively on the links between climate and security
Supports a Council role and the draft as an important FIRST step, without inventing a later vote.

Retains meaningful inclusion of women and girls disproportionately affected by conflict and climate.
in particular with respect to women and girls, who suffer disproportionately from conflict and climate change, so that they can play a meaningful role.
9138-IND: Calls for immediate cessation of hostilities, dialogue, diplomacy and return to negotiations.

Affirms international law, Charter, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
We firmly believe that the global order should be anchored in international law, the Charter of the United Nations and respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of States.
